asDecan.p: There's a thin crescent moon in the top corner of the Two of Swords, and it's there for a reason. Your Sun is in the first ten degrees of Libra, and the Golden Dawn gave that stretch to the Moon. The Moon has no special standing in Libra. It's neither helped nor held back there, so it takes its cue from Venus, who rules the sign. What you get is Libra at its freshest, cardinal air that likes to start things and wants them fair, with the Moon's moods going on quietly under all the reasoning. Next along is the Three, Saturn's slice, where Libra learns about fairness through loss, and then the Four, Jupiter's, which knows how to rest. Justice is your Sun card and covers the whole sign. The Two is just your ten degrees. The Moon's own Major is The High Priestess, and I often see a bit of her in people born here, who know more about how everyone's feeling than they let on.

You can tell when a room has gone off. Someone's tone shifts in a work meeting and you've registered it before they've finished the sentence, and you spend the rest of the hour adjusting what you say to bring it back level. At a family dinner you're the one who changes the subject when your dad and your sister start on politics. Picking a restaurant for a group can take you twenty minutes of texts, because you're honestly trying to find somewhere that suits everyone, the vegetarian included, and the friend who's short on money this month. When a friend asks what you think of her new boyfriend, you give her a very balanced answer and then lie awake wondering if it was the true one. Your mood follows whoever you live with more than you'd like, and a tense house tires you out faster than a long day at work does.

What people don't notice so much is your timing. The Moon gives you a feel for when someone's ready to hear a thing, and Libra gives you the words, so you tend to raise the difficult subject at the right moment, in the car on the way home or over the washing up, when nobody has to look anyone in the eye. In a fight at work about the roster, you're usually the one who sees it's really about somebody feeling overlooked, and you say so gently enough that nobody gets defensive. I've seen this a lot with early Libra Suns. Counsellors train for years to do it, and you mostly picked it up at the family dinner table without anyone noticing, including you. People end up telling you things they haven't told their partners.

The part that's easy to miss is that when you don't decide, someone else does, and it's usually whoever pushes hardest. The holiday gets booked by the friend who cared least where you went. The job offer lapses while you're still making a list. You say 'whatever you think' to your partner and mean it, and three weeks later you're quietly annoyed about the result and can't say so, because you did say whatever. And when you're really upset, you can go very calm and very polite, arms folded, answering in full sentences. It's hard for anyone to argue with that or get past it. People close to you do learn that the politeness is the warning sign, but it takes them a while, and until then they think everything's fine.

Something goes wrong, a job falls through, a parent ends up in hospital, a friend goes cold on you, and your first move is to look after everyone else's feelings about it. You ring round, you keep your voice even, and people tell you how well you're handling it. A week later it turns up at three in the morning. You're going over both sides again, you've asked four friends what they'd do, and you've half agreed with all of them. With the Moon here your sleep and your appetite are usually the first things to slip, so watch those. It's hard on the people around you, because they can't tell where you stand and you keep being reasonable at them. What helps is telling one person how you feel before you've checked whether the feeling is fair. Then eat something decent, get a proper night's sleep, and decide in the morning.

Early in a relationship you go along with a lot, their friends, their takeaway, their idea of a good Sunday, partly because being easy feels like being kind and partly because the Moon here means you really do pick up their mood as if it were your own. Then about a year in, your own tastes start turning up, and your partner is a bit surprised to meet you. The less obvious thing is how much you need looking after in plain ways. The Moon is about being fed, being warm, having someone notice you're tired, and you can be so busy making the evening nice for the other person that nobody notices you skipped dinner. When you're asked something that matters, try 'let me think about it and tell you tomorrow'. They'll get a truer answer, and you won't be stuck with a yes you didn't mean.

You do well wherever you stand between two groups who don't quite understand each other. A school office, account management, wedding planning, interior design, the front desk of a busy clinic, anywhere the client wants one thing and the people doing the work want another and you're the one who makes it sound like the same thing. Managers often send you to deliver the bad news because it lands better from you, and that belongs in your pay review as well as in their thanks. The trouble spot is any job where you have to choose between two good options on a deadline, which supplier, which candidate, which proposal goes forward. You'll want more information and one more meeting. Plenty of early Libras do their best work alongside a colleague who likes deciding, someone who'll say 'right, this one' once you've laid out the case. Find that person and make it a proper arrangement.

At twenty this decan often takes its shape from whoever's close. You like the music your partner likes, you study what your parents think is sensible, and if someone asks what you want for dinner you honestly don't know. By the mid-thirties something has usually made the choice for you once too often, a relationship that ended on the other person's terms or a job you drifted into and stayed in, and most people with the Sun here get firmer after that. They notice their own preferences earlier and say them sooner, sometimes a bit bluntly while they're getting the hang of it. In the fifties you often end up as the one the family runs through. You host the difficult Christmas, you know who isn't speaking to whom, and you can say 'I'd rather not' without explaining yourself for ten minutes afterwards.

Next time you're stuck between two options, give one heads and one tails and toss a coin. Before you look at the coin, and in the second after you do, notice what your stomach does. A little drop of disappointment or a small lift of relief is the preference you've been keeping from yourself. You don't have to do what the coin says. Try it for a couple of weeks on small things first, which film, which café, before you use it on anything that matters.
